code.title: Activity selection two ways: greedy O(N log N) vs DP O(N^2)
code.python:
meetings = [(4, 7), (1, 3), (8, 10), (2, 5), (6, 9)]
# Both methods start by sorting the meetings by end time.
meetings.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])
print("Meetings by end time: " + " ".join(f"({s},{e})" for s, e in meetings))

# Greedy: one pass, one choice per meeting, never undone.
# Time O(N log N) for the sort, O(1) extra space.
count, last_end = 0, float("-inf")
for s, e in meetings:
    if s >= last_end:
        count += 1
        last_end = e

# DP: dp[i] = most meetings in a schedule whose last meeting is i.
# It tries every earlier meeting j. Time O(N^2), space O(N).
n = len(meetings)
dp = [1] * n
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(i):
        if meetings[j][1] <= meetings[i][0]:
            dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1)

print("Greedy answer:", count)
print("DP answer:", max(dp))

followUps:
Activity selection (pick the most meetings that do not overlap) is the standard example: both methods give the same answer, but greedy is much cheaper.

Greedy: sort by end time and keep each meeting that starts at or after the last kept end. That is O(N log N) time for the sort and O(1) extra space. DP: dp[i] = best schedule ending with meeting i, checking every earlier meeting, which is O(N2) time and O(N) space.

For (1,3), (2,5), (4,7), (6,9), (8,10) both return 3. For N = 100,000 greedy does about 2 million steps, while the simple DP does about 5 billion comparisons.

In practice yes: a greedy is a DP that looks at only one choice per step, so you can always write the slower version that tries every choice and keeps the best. It returns the same answer because the greedy choice is one of the choices it tries.

Example: activity selection as a DP tries every earlier meeting for each meeting (O(N2)); the greedy keeps just the earliest-ending one (O(N log N)).

The catch is cost. For some greedy problems the natural DP state is a whole set of items (Huffman's set of unmerged trees, a spanning tree's set of chosen edges), so the DP is exponential and useless. The reverse is not true: most DPs, such as 0/1 knapsack, have no correct greedy.

code.title: Check a greedy against brute force on small inputs

followUps:
You show that any best schedule can be changed, one meeting at a time, into the greedy schedule without losing a meeting.

  1. Let g be the meeting that ends first overall (the greedy pick). Take any optimal schedule and let f be its first meeting.
  2. g ends no later than f, so swapping f for g cannot clash with the rest, which all start after f ends. The count stays the same.
  3. Now both schedules start with g. Remove everything that overlaps g and repeat the argument on what is left.

Example: optimal = (2,5), (6,9); greedy first pick = (1,3). Swap to get (1,3), (6,9): still 2 meetings and still valid. So greedy is never behind an optimal schedule.

You measure how far each solution can reach after k jumps and show that greedy's reach is never smaller than anyone else's.

Let Rk be the farthest index greedy can reach with k jumps: R0 = 0 and Rk+1 = the largest i + nums[i] over all i ≤ Rk. Claim: any sequence of k jumps ends at an index ≤ Rk. Induction: if the other solution stands at p ≤ Rk after k jumps, its next landing is at most p + nums[p], which is one of the values inside the maximum, so it is ≤ Rk+1.

On [2,3,1,1,4]: R0 = 0, R1 = 2, R2 = 4. No one can reach index 4 in 1 jump because R1 = 2, so 2 jumps is optimal.

code.title: Activity selection: three sorting rules on two counterexamples

followUps:
Only the comparison changes: keep a meeting when its start is strictly greater than the last kept end, instead of greater than or equal.

Sorting by end time and the proof stay exactly the same, because the earliest-ending meeting still leaves the most room for the others.

Example: (1,3), (3,5), (6,8). If touching is allowed, start >= lastEnd keeps all 3. If it is not allowed, start > lastEnd rejects (3,5) and keeps 2. Cost is still O(N log N) time and O(1) extra space. In an interview, ask which rule applies before coding, since this one character decides the answer.

Then greedy no longer works and you need dynamic programming (this is called weighted interval scheduling).

Counterexample: (1,10) with profit 100, (1,2) with profit 10, (3,4) with profit 10. Earliest-end greedy takes the two small meetings for 20; the best is 100.

Method: sort by end time. For meeting i, find with binary search p(i), the last meeting that ends at or before i starts. Then either skip i or take it:

dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1],
            profit[i] + dp[p(i)]);

Time O(N log N), space O(N).

code.title: Job sequencing: richest job first, latest free slot
code.python:
ids = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
deadline = [2, 1, 2, 1, 3]
profit = [100, 19, 27, 25, 15]
n, max_d = len(ids), 3
print("Jobs (deadline, profit): " + " ".join(f"{ids[i]}({deadline[i]},{profit[i]})" for i in range(n)))

# Look at the jobs from the highest profit to the lowest.
order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: -profit[i])

slot = [None] * (max_d + 1)   # slot[t] = job done in hour t
total = 0
for j in order:
    # Walk back from the deadline to find the latest free hour.
    t = deadline[j]
    while t >= 1 and slot[t] is not None:
        t -= 1
    if t >= 1:
        slot[t] = ids[j]
        total += profit[j]
        print(f"Take {ids[j]} -> slot {t}")
    else:
        print(f"Skip {ids[j]}")

# Time O(N log N + N * D), space O(D). Union-find makes it O(N log N).
print("Schedule: " + " ".join(s if s else "-" for s in slot[1:]))
print("Total profit:", total)

followUps:
Because the sets of jobs that can all finish on time obey the two matroid rules, which is exactly what makes “richest first” safe.

A set of unit-time jobs is feasible when, for every hour t, at most t of its jobs have deadline ≤ t.

  • Hereditary: removing a job from a feasible set only lowers those counts, so every subset is feasible.
  • Exchange: if feasible set A has more jobs than feasible set B, some job of A can be added to B and B stays feasible (pick one whose deadline lies after the last hour where B is at least as crowded as A).

Example: A = {d=1, d=2}, B = {d=1}. Adding A's d=2 job to B gives a set that is still on time.

You stop using an array with one cell per time slot, because 109 cells is far too much memory. Two standard fixes:

  • Cap the deadline: with N jobs only N slots can ever be used, so replace each deadline by min(d, N) and run the usual algorithm.
  • Sort by deadline and keep a min-heap of profits: add each job; if the heap now holds more jobs than the deadline allows, drop the cheapest.
sort jobs by deadline;
for (job : jobs) {
  heap.add(job.profit);
  if (heap.size() > job.deadline) heap.poll();
}
answer = sum of heap;

Jobs (d=1, 40), (d=2, 50), (d=2, 60): the heap ends as {50, 60}, profit 110. Time O(N log N), space O(N).

code.title: Ratio greedy: right for fractional knapsack, wrong for 0/1
code.python:
from functools import cmp_to_key

value, weight = [100, 120, 60], [20, 30, 10]
cap, n = 50, 3
print(f"Capacity {cap}, items (value, weight): " + " ".join(f"({value[i]},{weight[i]})" for i in range(n)))

# Sort by value per kg, best first. Cross-multiply to avoid doubles.
order = sorted(range(n), key=cmp_to_key(lambda a, b: value[b] * weight[a] - value[a] * weight[b]))

# Fractional: take whole items, then a slice of the first that does not fit.
frac, left = 0.0, cap
for i in order:
    take = min(left, weight[i])
    frac += value[i] * take / weight[i]
    left -= take

# 0/1 with the same rule: an item is taken whole or not at all.
greedy01, left = 0, cap
for i in order:
    if weight[i] <= left:
        greedy01 += value[i]
        left -= weight[i]

# 0/1 done properly with DP: dp[w] = best value with capacity w.
dp = [0] * (cap + 1)
for i in range(n):
    for w in range(cap, weight[i] - 1, -1):
        dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - weight[i]] + value[i])

# Greedy: O(N log N) time, O(N) space. DP: O(N * W) time, O(W) space.
print(f"Fractional greedy: {frac:.2f}")
print("0/1 ratio greedy:", greedy01)
print("0/1 DP (optimal):", dp[cap])

followUps:
Yes, on average: you can skip the full sort and use the quickselect idea on the value-per-kg ratio.

  1. Pick a pivot ratio and split the items into “better than pivot” and “not better”.
  2. Add up the weight of the better group. If it is more than the capacity, the answer lies inside that group, so repeat there.
  3. Otherwise take the whole better group, lower the capacity by its weight, and repeat on the other group.

Each round throws away about half of the items, so the work is N + N/2 + N/4 + … ≈ 2N, which is O(N) expected time (O(N) worst case with median-of-medians) and O(1) extra space if done in place. Example: capacity 50, ratios 6, 5, 4 with weights 10, 20, 30; pivot 5 gives a better group of weight 10 ≤ 50, so take it and continue with capacity 40.

Plain ratio greedy gives no guarantee at all, but one small fix guarantees at least half of the best value.

Bad case: capacity 100, item A (value 2, weight 1) and item B (value 100, weight 100). A has the better ratio, so greedy takes it, B no longer fits, and the result is 2 instead of 100.

Fix: return the larger of (a) the greedy total and (b) the single most valuable item that fits. This is always ≥ half of the optimum, because the greedy items plus the first item that did not fit are worth at least the fractional optimum, which is itself ≥ the 0/1 optimum. In the example the fix returns 100. Cost stays O(N log N). If you need to be closer, an FPTAS reaches (1 − ε) of the optimum in time polynomial in N and 1/ε.

code.title: Huffman cost: keep merging the two smallest frequencies
code.python:
freq = sorted([45, 13, 9, 5, 16, 12])
print("Frequencies (sorted): " + " ".join(map(str, freq)))

# Two queues instead of a heap: sorted leaves, and merged nodes.
# Merged sums come out in rising order, so both queues stay sorted
# and the two smallest nodes are always at the two fronts.
n = len(freq)
merged = []
i = j = total = 0
for _ in range(n - 1):
    pair = []
    for _ in range(2):
        # Take the smaller front of the two queues.
        if i < n and (j >= len(merged) or freq[i] <= merged[j]):
            pair.append(freq[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            pair.append(merged[j])
            j += 1
    s = pair[0] + pair[1]
    merged.append(s)
    total += s   # every merge adds one bit to all symbols below it
    print(f"Merge {pair[0]} + {pair[1]} = {s}")

# Time O(N log N) for the sort, then O(N); space O(N).
print("Total bits:", total)

followUps:
A canonical Huffman code keeps only the code length of each symbol from the Huffman tree and then hands out the actual bit patterns by a fixed rule, so the decoder can rebuild the code without receiving the tree.

Rule: sort symbols by (length, symbol). The first code is all zeros. Each next code is the previous code plus 1, with zeros added on the right whenever the length grows.

Example with lengths A=1, B=2, C=3, D=3: A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111.

The file header only stores the lengths (a few bits per symbol) instead of a tree, and decoding can use small lookup tables. DEFLATE (zip, gzip, PNG) and JPEG work this way. The total number of bits is the same as with any other Huffman code.

Huffman is always less than 1 bit per symbol above the entropy: H ≤ average code length < H + 1.

It is exactly equal to the entropy when every probability is a power of 1/2 (for example 1/2, 1/4, 1/4 gives lengths 1, 2, 2 and 1.5 bits either way). The gap is largest when one symbol dominates, because no code can be shorter than 1 bit.

Example: probabilities 0.9 and 0.1. Entropy is about 0.47 bits per symbol, but Huffman must spend 1 bit per symbol, more than twice as much.

To close the gap, encode blocks of several symbols as one symbol (the extra cost drops to less than 1/k bits per symbol for blocks of k), or use arithmetic coding or ANS, which get within a tiny fraction of the entropy.

Treat it as a special case and give that one character a 1-bit code such as 0.

With one character the heap has a single node, so no merge happens and the leaf is also the root at depth 0. A naive walk of the tree would then assign an empty code, the encoded text would have 0 bits, and the decoder could not tell how many characters there were.

if (heap.size() == 1) {
  code.put(onlyChar, "0");
  return freq[onlyChar];   // total bits
}

Example: “aaaa” becomes 0000, 4 bits. Also handle the empty string (0 bits, no tree). Both are O(1) checks before the normal O(N log N) loop.

code.title: Minimum meeting rooms: sorted starts and ends, two pointers
code.python:
meetings = [(900, 910), (940, 1200), (950, 1120), (1100, 1130), (1500, 1900), (1800, 2000)]
print("Meetings: " + " ".join(f"({s},{e})" for s, e in meetings))

# Sort the start times and the end times separately.
start = sorted(s for s, _ in meetings)
end = sorted(e for _, e in meetings)

n = len(meetings)
rooms = best = i = j = 0
while i < n:
    if start[i] < end[j]:
        # A meeting starts before the earliest one ends: one more room.
        rooms += 1
        i += 1
        best = max(best, rooms)
    else:
        # A meeting has ended (touching counts as free): release a room.
        rooms -= 1
        j += 1

# Time O(N log N) for the sorts, space O(N).
print("Rooms needed:", best)

followUps:
Sort the meetings by start time and keep a min-heap of busy rooms ordered by the time each becomes free; reuse the room that frees up first, otherwise open a new one.

sort meetings by start;
for (m : meetings) {
  if (!heap.isEmpty() && heap.peek().end <= m.start)
    room[m.id] = heap.poll().room;   // reuse
  else room[m.id] = nextRoom++;       // new room
  heap.add(new Busy(m.end, room[m.id]));
}

Example: (0,30), (5,10), (15,20). (0,30) gets room 0; (5,10) gets room 1; at 15 the heap top is (10, room 1), which is free, so (15,20) reuses room 1. Answer [0, 1, 1] with 2 rooms. Time O(N log N), space O(N).

Use a sorted map of time points (a TreeMap) holding +1 at each start and −1 at each end, or a segment tree if queries must also be fast.

  • Sorted map: adding a meeting is two O(log N) updates. The number of rooms is the largest running sum when you walk the map in time order, which is O(N) per query.
  • Segment tree with lazy “add 1 to a range” and “maximum of all”: each new meeting adds 1 on [start, end) and the answer is the root's maximum, so both are O(log N). Build it over compressed coordinates or create nodes on demand.

Example: add (10,20) → max 1; add (15,25) → max 2; add (20,30) → still 2, because 20 is an end before it is a start.

code.title: Gas Station: reset the start when the tank goes negative
code.python:
gas, cost = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]
print("gas:  " + " ".join(map(str, gas)))
print("cost: " + " ".join(map(str, cost)))

total = tank = start = 0
for i in range(len(gas)):
    gain = gas[i] - cost[i]   # fuel won or lost on this leg
    total += gain
    tank += gain
    if tank < 0:
        # No station from start to i can be the answer: skip them all.
        print(f"Tank below zero after station {i}, restart at {i + 1}")
        start = i + 1
        tank = 0

# If the whole circle loses fuel, no start can work.
answer = -1 if total < 0 else start
# Time O(N), space O(1).
print("Total gain:", total)
print("Start station:", answer)

followUps:
It is the deepest the tank would go below zero if you started with nothing: max(0, −(smallest running sum of gas − cost)).

Walk the stations in order from 0, keep a running sum of gains, and remember its lowest value. Starting with exactly that much extra fuel lifts the whole curve so it just touches zero.

int sum = 0, low = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  sum += gas[i] - cost[i];
  low = Math.min(low, sum);
}
return -low;

Example: gains [−2, −2, −2, 3, 3] give running sums −2, −4, −6, −3, 0. The lowest is −6, so you need 6 units at the start. Time O(N), space O(1).

The fuelling step becomes tank = min(cap, tank + gas[i]) - cost[i], and the shortcut “total gas ≥ total cost means a start exists” is no longer true, because fuel that does not fit in the tank is lost.

Example: gas [5, 0], cost [1, 3], capacity 3. Total gain is +1, yet from station 0 you can hold only 3, arrive at station 1 with 2 and cannot pay 3. No start works.

The skip rule survives: arriving somewhere with more fuel is never worse, so if a start s fails at i, every start between them fails too. So simulate over the circle written twice (2N legs), restart at i + 1 on each failure, and accept a start once it has completed N legs in a row; if the start index passes N − 1, return −1. Time O(N), space O(1).

code.title: Jump Game II: farthest-jump greedy vs level-by-level greedy
code.python:
def farthest_jump(nums):
    # Wrong greedy: always land as far as the current jump allows.
    i, jumps, n = 0, 0, len(nums)
    while i < n - 1:
        i = min(n - 1, i + nums[i])
        jumps += 1
    return jumps


def levels(nums):
    # Right greedy: cur_end = last index reachable with the jumps used so far,
    # farthest = last index reachable with one more jump.
    jumps = cur_end = farthest = 0
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
        farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])
        if i == cur_end:      # this level is finished: one more jump
            jumps += 1
            cur_end = farthest
    return jumps


nums = [2, 3, 1, 1, 4]
print("nums: " + " ".join(map(str, nums)))
# Both run in O(N) time and O(1) space; only the second is optimal.
print(f"Farthest-jump greedy: {farthest_jump(nums)} jumps")
print(f"Level-by-level greedy: {levels(nums)} jumps")

followUps:
Remember which index gave the farthest reach in each level; those indices, followed by the last index, are the path.

for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
  if (i + nums[i] > farthest) { farthest = i + nums[i]; best = i; }
  if (i == curEnd) { path.add(best); curEnd = farthest; }
}
path.add(n - 1);

On [2,3,1,1,4]: at i = 0 the best is index 0 (reach 2), so the path starts [0]. At i = 1 the reach becomes 4 with best = 1; at i = 2 the level ends and 1 is added. Final path 0 → 1 → 4, 2 jumps.

It is valid because each recorded index lies inside the previous level, so the index recorded before it can reach it. Time O(N), extra space O(answer length).

Both are “cover a line with the fewest intervals”, and that is Jump Game II once you store, for every left end, the farthest right end you can reach from it.

  1. Turn each tap i with range r into the interval [max(0, i − r), min(n, i + r)]; a video clip is already an interval [start, end].
  2. Build reach[left] = max(right).
  3. Run the level scan: farthest = max(farthest, reach[i]); when i == curEnd, count one more interval and set curEnd = farthest. If farthest did not move past i, there is a gap: return −1.

Example: n = 5, ranges [3,4,1,1,0,0]. Tap 1 covers [0,5], so reach[0] = 5 and the answer is 1. Time O(N + number of intervals), space O(N).

code.title: Coin change: largest-coin greedy fails, DP finds the fewest coins

followUps:
A canonical coin system is a set of coins for which “take the largest coin that fits” gives the fewest coins for every amount. {1, 5, 10, 25} is canonical; {1, 3, 4} is not, because 6 = 3 + 3 beats 4 + 1 + 1.

Simple test: if greedy ever fails, the smallest failing amount is below the sum of the two largest coins. So compute the DP answer and the greedy answer for every amount up to that sum and compare.

For {1, 3, 4} check amounts 1 to 7: they agree up to 5, and at 6 greedy says 3 while DP says 2, so the system is not canonical. This costs O(C × coins) time where C is the largest coin. A faster O(coins3) test by Pearson exists, but the simple one is enough in an interview.

It fills a table where dp[x] is the fewest coins that make amount x, using the answers for smaller amounts.

The last coin used to make x must be some coin c; the rest is the best way to make x − c. Try every coin and keep the smallest result. dp[0] = 0, and unreachable amounts stay at infinity.

dp[0] = 0;
for (int x = 1; x <= amount; x++)
  for (int c : coins)
    if (c <= x) dp[x] = Math.min(dp[x], dp[x - c] + 1);

Coins {1, 3, 4}: dp for 0..6 is 0, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2. So 6 needs 2 coins (3 + 3). Time O(amount × coins), space O(amount).

code.title: Matroid greedy: heaviest edge first, add if no cycle (Kruskal)
code.python:
parent = [0, 1, 2, 3]


def find(x):
    # Union-find "find": the representative of x's connected group.
    while parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
        x = parent[x]
    return x


# Edges (u, v, weight) on 4 nodes. Independent set = edges with no cycle.
edges = [(1, 2, 5), (0, 1, 7), (1, 3, 3), (0, 2, 6), (2, 3, 4)]

# The matroid greedy: heaviest first ...
edges.sort(key=lambda e: -e[2])
total = 0
for u, v, w in edges:
    a, b = find(u), find(v)
    label = f"Edge {u}-{v} weight {w}: "
    # ... and add the edge only if the set stays independent.
    if a != b:
        parent[a] = b
        total += w
        print(label + "add")
    else:
        print(label + "skip (cycle)")

# Time O(E log E), space O(V).
print("Maximum-weight spanning tree:", total)

followUps:
Take two on-time job sets A and B with A larger; you can always find a job in A that B can accept and still finish everything on time.

Write Nt(S) for the number of jobs in S with deadline ≤ t. S is feasible exactly when Nt(S) ≤ t for every t.

  1. Let k be the largest t with Nt(B) ≥ Nt(A). It exists (t = 0) and is below the last deadline because |A| > |B|.
  2. Then A has more jobs with deadline exactly k + 1 than B has, so pick such a job x that is not in B.
  3. B + x is feasible: for t ≤ k nothing changed; for t > k, Nt(B) + 1 ≤ Nt(A) ≤ t.

Example: A has deadlines {1, 2, 3}, B has {1, 3}. Here k = 1, and A's deadline-2 job goes into B.

It is the family of sets that are independent in two matroids at the same time, and greedy is not enough because that family is usually not a matroid: the exchange rule breaks.

Bipartite matching is the classic case. Matroid 1: no two chosen edges share a left node. Matroid 2: no two share a right node. A matching obeys both.

Example with edges a–x, a–y, b–x: greedy may pick a–x first, after which nothing else fits, giving 1 edge. The best is {a–y, b–x} with 2 edges. Greedy cannot recover, because it never removes a choice.

The fix is augmenting paths that swap elements in and out (Edmonds' matroid intersection algorithm), which is still polynomial time. With three matroids the problem becomes NP-hard.

code.title: Comparator pitfalls: a - b overflow, and the Largest Number order
code.python:
from functools import cmp_to_key

a, b = 2000000000, -2000000000
print(f"a = {a}, b = {b}")
# Bug: a - b does not fit in 32 bits, so it wraps to a negative number
# and the comparator claims a < b. Python ints never overflow, so we
# reproduce the 32-bit wrap-around by hand.
diff = (a - b + 2**31) % 2**32 - 2**31
print(f"a - b in 32 bits = {diff} (negative: wrongly says a < b)")
# Fix: compare without subtracting.
safe = (a > b) - (a < b)
print(f"Safe compare = {safe} (correct: a > b)")

# Largest Number: put x before y when the text x+y is bigger than y+x.
nums = ["3", "30", "34", "5", "9"]
print("Numbers: " + " ".join(nums))
# Both strings have the same length, so text order equals number order.
nums.sort(key=cmp_to_key(lambda x, y: (y + x > x + y) - (y + x < x + y)))
# Time O(N log N) comparisons of short strings, space O(N).
print("Largest number: " + "".join(nums))

followUps:
It is transitive because the rule “x before y when x+y > y+x” is the same as comparing one fixed number per string, and ordinary number comparison is transitive.

Let x have a digits and y have b digits. As numbers, x+y = x·10b + y and y+x = y·10a + x. So:

x·10b + y > y·10a + x ⇔ x·(10b − 1) > y·(10a − 1) ⇔ x / (10a − 1) > y / (10b − 1).

Each side now depends on one string only. That key is the string repeated forever as a decimal: 3 → 0.333…, 30 → 0.3030…, 34 → 0.3434…. Since 0.3434 > 0.3333 > 0.3030, the order is 34, 3, 30, and if x beats y and y beats z, then x beats z.

Because objects need a stable sort and have expensive comparisons, while primitives need neither and benefit most from raw speed and low memory.

  • Objects (TimSort): two objects can be “equal” for the comparator yet differ in other fields, so their original order must be kept (stable). TimSort is stable, uses few comparisons (each one is a method call), is close to O(N) on partly sorted data, and is O(N log N) in the worst case. It needs up to N/2 extra references.
  • Primitives (dual-pivot quicksort): two equal int values cannot be told apart, so stability means nothing. Quicksort works in place with good cache use and only O(log N) stack. Its O(N2) worst case is guarded by fallbacks in the JDK.

Example: sorting people by age keeps two 30-year-olds in input order only with the stable sort.

code.title: Stress test: random inputs, greedy vs brute-force DP, stop at first mismatch

followUps:
A stress test needs four parts: a random small-input generator, your fast solution, a slow but obviously correct brute force, and a loop that stops at the first disagreement and prints the input.

Random rnd = new Random(1);            // fixed seed: failures repeat
for (int t = 0; t < 100000; t++) {
  int[] a = randomArray(rnd, 1 + rnd.nextInt(8), 10);
  int fast = greedy(a), slow = brute(a);
  if (fast != slow) { print(a, fast, slow); break; }
}

Keep sizes tiny (N ≤ 8, values ≤ 10): small inputs hit ties and edge cases far more often, the brute force (all 2N subsets) stays fast, and a failing case is short enough to trace by hand. Example: for coins {1, 3, 4} this finds amount 6 (greedy 3, brute 2) on the fifth trial of the program above.

Read it against a short checklist, then test it mechanically instead of trusting how it looks.

  • Subtraction: a - b overflows for large values; require Integer.compare.
  • Doubles: no (int)(x - y) casts (0.7 becomes 0); compare ratios by cross-multiplying in long.
  • Contract: compare(a, b) and compare(b, a) must have opposite signs, equal items must return 0, and the order must be transitive.
  • Ties: is the tie-break the one the problem needs?

Then run a property test: for random triples, including Integer.MIN_VALUE, MAX_VALUE and duplicates, assert those three rules. Example: with a - b, the pair (2,000,000,000, −2,000,000,000) returns a negative number and the test fails immediately.

code.title: Cache eviction: LRU (greedy heuristic) vs Belady's offline optimum
code.python:
def lru(pages, cap):
    # LRU: evict the page that was used longest ago. Needs only the past.
    frames, faults = [], 0   # least recent first
    for p in pages:
        if p in frames:
            frames.remove(p)   # hit: now most recent
            frames.append(p)
            continue
        faults += 1
        if len(frames) == cap:
            frames.pop(0)
        frames.append(p)
    return faults


def belady(pages, cap):
    # Belady: evict the page whose next use is furthest away. Needs the future.
    frames, faults, n = [], 0, len(pages)
    for i in range(n):
        if pages[i] in frames:
            continue
        faults += 1
        if len(frames) == cap:
            victim, far = 0, -1
            for k in range(cap):
                nxt = i + 1   # position of the next use of frame k
                while nxt < n and pages[nxt] != frames[k]:
                    nxt += 1
                if nxt > far:
                    far, victim = nxt, k
            frames.pop(victim)
        frames.append(pages[i])
    return faults


pages = [7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 7, 0, 1]
print("Pages: " + " ".join(map(str, pages)))
print("Cache size: 3")
# LRU is O(N * C) here; this simple Belady is O(N^2 * C). Space O(C).
print("LRU misses:", lru(pages, 3))
print("Belady (optimal) misses:", belady(pages, 3))

followUps:
Belady's rule is optimal because throwing out the item that will be needed furthest in the future can never cause an earlier miss than any other choice, and it is impractical because a real cache does not know the future.

Why optimal (exchange argument): take any other eviction plan. At the first point where it evicts a different item, switch it to Belady's choice. The item Belady evicts is needed later than the other one, so up to that later moment the switched plan has no extra miss; repeat for every difference.

Example: cache holds 7, 0, 1 and the next requests are 2, 0, 3, 0, 4. Page 7 is never used again, so evict 7.

In practice it is used offline, on a recorded trace, as the best possible score. On the classic 20-request trace with 3 slots, Belady has 9 misses and LRU has 12. LRU guesses the future from the past.

When the exact answer costs more than it is worth: it is too slow or too big for the input, or the input itself is only an estimate.

  • Size: 0/1 knapsack with N = 100,000 items and capacity 109 needs about 1014 DP steps; the ratio greedy with the “best single item” fix needs about 2 million and is guaranteed at least half of the optimum.
  • Hard problems: bin packing and set cover are NP-hard, so exact methods do not scale; first-fit decreasing uses at most about 11/9 of the optimal number of bins.
  • Time limits and online input: a scheduler must decide in microseconds, before all jobs are known.
  • Noisy data: if profits are forecasts with 10% error, a 2% better plan is not real.

Ask for a proven bound, measure the gap against the exact DP on small cases, and keep the exact method when mistakes are costly.
